obedience.e: From Middle English obedience, from Anglo-Norman obedience, from Old French obedience (modern French obédience), from Latin oboedientia.

obedient.e: From Middle English obedient, from Old French obedient, from Latin oboediēns, present active participle of oboediō (“obey”).
obedient.g: Willing to comply with the commands, orders, or instructions of those in authority; biddable.

obeisance.e: From Middle English obeisaunce (“obedience, obeisance”), from Old French obeïssance, derived from obeïssant (“obedient”), participle of obeïr (“to obey”), from Latin oboediō, obēdiō; ob- (“to, for”) + audiō (“to hear”).
obeisance.g: Demonstration of an obedient attitude, especially by bowing deeply; a deep bow which demonstrates such an attitude.

obese.e: From Latin obēsus, derived from obedō (“to devour, eat away”), from ob (“away”) + edō (“to eat”).
obese.g: Extremely overweight, especially: weighing more than 20% (for men) or 25% (for women) over their conventionally ideal weight determined by h

obey.e: From Middle English obeyen, from Anglo-Norman obeir, obeier et al., Old French obeir, from Latin oboediō (also obēdiō (“to listen to, harken, usually in extended sense, obey, be subject to, serve”)), from ob- (“before, near”) + audiō (“to hear”).
obey.g: To do as ordered by (a person, institution etc), to act according to the bidding of.

object.e: From Old French object, from Medieval Latin obiectum (“object”, literally “thrown against”), from obiectus, perfect passive participle of obiciō (“to throw against”), from ob- (“against”) + iaciō (“to throw”), as a calque of Ancient Greek ἀντικείμενον (antikeímenon).
object.g: A thing that has physical existence but is not alive.

objection.e: From Middle French objection, from Old French objeccion, from Latin obiectio. Equivalent to object + -ion.

oblation.e: From Middle English oblacioun, from Old French oblacion, from Latin oblātiō (“offering”), from offerō (“to offer, present”). By surface analysis, oblate + -ion.
oblation.g: The offering of worship, thanks etc. to a deity.

obligate.e: Partly inherited from Middle English obligat(e) (“bound (by any obligation), obliged”), partly directly borrowed from Latin obligātus, see Etymology 1, -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more.
obligate.g: Requiring a (specified) way of life, habitat, etc.

obligation.e: From Middle English obligacioun, from Old French obligacion, from Latin obligatio, obligationem, from obligatum (past participle of obligare), from ob- (“to”) + ligare (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).
obligation.g: The act of binding oneself by a social, legal, or moral tie to someone.

obliterated.e: From obliterate + -ed (suffix forming adjectives; and past tenses and past participles of regular verbs).

oblivion.e: From Middle English oblivion, from Anglo-Norman oblivion, from Latin oblīviō (“forgetfulness”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).
oblivion.g: The state of forgetting completely, of being oblivious, unconscious, unaware, as when sleeping, drunk, or dead.

oblivious.e: From Middle English oblivious, from Latin oblīviōsus (“forgetful, oblivious”), formed from oblīvium (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) + -ōsus (“full of, overly, prone to”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).
oblivious.g: Lacking awareness; unmindful; unaware, unconscious of.

obscure.e: From Middle English obscure, from Old French obscur, from Latin obscūrus (“dark, dusky, indistinct”), from ob- + *scūrus, from Proto-Italic *skoiros, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃-.

obscurity.e: From Middle English obscurite, obscuryte, from Middle French obscurité and its etymon Latin obscūritās. By surface analysis, obscure + -ity.

observation.e: From Middle English observacion, borrowed from Middle French observacion. Morphologically observe + -ation.
observation.g: The act of observing, and the fact of being observed (see observance)

observe.e: From Middle French observer, from Old French observer, from Latin observō (“to watch”), from ob- (“before”) + servō (“to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to guard”).
observe.g: To notice or view, especially carefully or with attention to detail.

obsolete.e: Borrowed from Latin obsolētus (“worn out, gone out of use”), past participle of obsolēscere (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”); see obsolesce.
obsolete.g: No longer in use or no longer useful; now disused or neglected (often in favour of something newer, better, or more fashionable); outmoded.

obstacle.e: From Middle English obstacle, from Old French obstacle, from Latin obstāculum.
obstacle.g: Something that impedes, stands in the way of, or holds up progress, either physically or figuratively

obstinate.e: From Middle English obstinat(e) (“obstinate, stubborn”), from Latin obstinātus, perfect passive participle of obstinō (“set one's mind firmly upon, resolve”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ob (“before”) + *stinare, from stare (“to stand”).
obstinate.g: Stubbornly adhering to an opinion, purpose, or course, usually with implied unreasonableness; persistent.

obstruct.e: From Latin past participle stem obstruct- (“blocked up”), from verb obstruere, from ob (“against”) + struere (“pile up, build”).
obstruct.g: To block or fill (a passage) with obstacles or an obstacle.

obtain.e: From Middle English obteinen, from Anglo-Norman obtenir, optiner et al., and Middle French obtenir, from Latin obtinēre (“to gain, achieve, succeed, possess”), from ob- + tenēre (“to hold”).
obtain.g: To get hold of; to gain possession of, to procure; to acquire, in any way.

obvious.e: 16th century, from Latin obvius (“being in the way so as to meet, meeting, easy to access, at hand, ready, obvious”) + -ous, from ob- (“before”) + via (“way”).
obvious.g: Easily discovered, seen, or understood; self-explanatory.
